details:
**Kemmerich's boots**
Franz Kemmerich is a schoolmate of the protagonist whose leg is amputated; he dies of gangrene in a field hospital. His fine leather boots pass to Müller. After Müller is killed, the boots pass to the narrator, Paul Bäumer, so they track the deaths of the comrades.

**Gérard Duval**
Gérard Duval is a French soldier and a printer by trade. Paul stabs him during hand-to-hand fighting in a shell-hole and is trapped with him as he slowly dies. Paul repeats "forgive me, comrade" to the corpse and finds photos of Duval's wife and child in his pocketbook.

**Kantorek and the "Iron Youth"**
Kantorek is the patriotic schoolmaster whose speeches pressure Paul's class to enlist. He later sends a letter calling them the "Iron Youth," which makes them smile bitterly. When Kantorek is conscripted, his former student Mittelstaedt mocks his ill-fitting uniform and drills him with the phrase "Inadequate, quite inadequate."

**Stanislaus Katczinsky (Kat)**
Kat is the resourceful 40-year-old former cobbler who mentors Paul and has a "sixth sense" for finding food. He steals and roasts a goose with Paul. Paul carries him to safety after a leg wound, but Kat is killed by a shell splinter during the trip, and Paul loses his will to survive.

**Corporal Himmelstoss**
Himmelstoss is a former postman and the brutal drill corporal who torments the recruits during training, earning the nickname "terror of Klosterberg." Tjaden and others ambush him, throw a bedsheet over his head, and whip him in revenge. He later becomes friendlier, and at the front he carries the mortally wounded Haie Westhus to safety.

**"All quiet on the Western Front" army report**
The title comes from the novel's final page. Paul is killed in October 1918, near the end of the war, on a day so quiet that the army report says only that there is nothing new to report. In German this phrase is "Im Westen nichts Neues."

**Tjaden**
Tjaden is a hungry former locksmith and bed-wetter. Himmelstoss tries to "cure" him by making him share a bunk with another bed-wetter, so that whoever sleeps below is soaked. Tjaden takes the lead in getting revenge on Himmelstoss, including whipping him and later farting at him.

**Swimming to the French women**
Paul, Leer, and Kropp see a poster at a tavern and then defy orders by swimming naked across a canal to spend the night with three French women. Leer is the group's ladies' man and is later killed alongside their commander, Bertinck.

**Detering and the cherry blossoms**
Detering is a peasant soldier who misses his wife and farm. He is distressed by wounded horses screaming on the battlefield and wants them shot. After seeing a blossoming cherry tree that reminds him of home, he carries off some branches and later deserts.

**Paul's leave and his dying mother**
On leave at home, Paul feels a sense of strangeness and alienation and learns that his mother is dying of cancer. Back at a camp guarding Russian prisoners of war, he shares his mother's potato cakes with the starving prisoners.

**Ginger and the rations for 150 men**
The novel opens with the company's cook, Ginger, who has prepared beef and haricot beans for 150 men. Only about 80 survivors returned from the front, so Ginger is pressured into handing the extra rations to the hungry soldiers.

**Kemmerich's watch and mother**
Kemmerich's watch is stolen as he lies dying, prompting the remark "nobody should carry as good a watch as that." On leave, Paul visits Kemmerich's mother and lies that her son was shot through the heart and died instantly. She asks Paul, "Why are you living then, when he is dead?"

**Lewandowski in the hospital**
Lewandowski is a bedridden older patient at the Catholic hospital whose wife visits him. His fellow patients guard the door and look away so the couple can make love. The same hospital section includes Josef Hamacher, who warns that no patient comes back from the "Death Room."

**The Road Back**
This is Remarque's sequel. It follows the soldier Ernst Birkholz and returning characters such as Tjaden as they struggle to readjust to civilian life in Germany after the war.

**Lewis Milestone's 1930 film adaptation**
This American film helped popularize the novel and won the Academy Award for Best Picture. It ends with Paul reaching out toward a butterfly before being shot by a sniper.
